families.s: HSE foundry shakeout, fettling and abrasive-blasting control guidance
families.t: knock-out, shakeout, fettling, blasting cabinets, silica, dust extraction, RPE, vibration, maintenance and surveillance
f: Foundry COSHH sheets cover knock-out, shakeout, fettling and abrasive blasting.
These tasks can release substantial silica-containing dust.
Dust extraction should control emissions at the source.
Small-casting blasting should use a suitable blasting cabinet.
RPE may be required in addition to extraction for residual exposure.
Fettling tools can create hand-arm vibration risk.
Extraction, cabinets and hand tools require planned maintenance.
Exposure monitoring and health surveillance should cover silica and vibration risks where applicable.
families.g: Shakeout and fettling risk depends on casting and sand, task energy and dust generation, enclosure and extraction, blasting cabinet integrity, hand-tool vibration, RPE, maintenance and surveillance.

families.s: HSE molten-metal water-contamination and explosion-prevention guidance
families.t: wet scrap, rain, drums, drying, visual checks, furnace charge, moulds, ladles, training, PPE and incident review
f: Water contamination of molten metal can cause explosions.
Wet scrap is a common route for water to enter a furnace.
Scrap should be stored dry where practicable.
Exposed scrap should be dried and visually checked before charging.
Drums in scrap should be drained so trapped liquid cannot enter the furnace.
Moulds, ladles and implements should be dry and correctly prepared.
Workers need information, training, supervision and suitable PPE for molten-metal hazards.
Molten-metal incidents should be investigated and lessons incorporated into controls.
families.g: Water-explosion risk depends on metal and temperature, scrap and container condition, moisture and weather, drying and inspection, charge method, mould and ladle preparation, training and supervision.

families.s: HSE molten-metal industry lifting and moving guidance
families.t: overhead cranes, ladles, loads, planning, competence, supervision, safe execution, routes, equipment condition and exclusion zones
f: Molten-metal industries use overhead cranes and other equipment to move varied loads.
Overhead-crane operations can expose people to serious injury.
Lifting operations must be planned properly.
People undertaking and directing the lift should be sufficiently competent.
Lifting operations should be supervised appropriately.
The operation should be carried out safely.
Routes, suspended loads and molten-metal areas should control unnecessary access.
Cranes, ladles, attachments and tracks should be inspected and maintained to prevent failure.
families.g: Molten-metal lifting risk depends on load and temperature, crane and attachment condition, route and occupancy, planning and supervision, competence, communication, exclusion zones and maintenance.

families.s: HSE molten-metal protective-clothing selection and maintenance guidance
families.t: risk assessment, splash levels, aluminium and iron performance classes, clothing selection, care, maintenance, training and supervision
f: Molten-metal PPE should be selected only after more effective controls have been considered.
Suitable protective clothing may be required where residual molten-metal exposure remains.
Successful use requires risk assessment, correct selection, care and maintenance, training and supervision.
HSE describes increasing incident levels from sparks to localised impact from large eruptions or explosions.
Clothing performance is tested differently for molten aluminium and molten iron splash.
Real incidents can differ from test conditions and should be considered in selection.
Damaged or contaminated clothing should be removed from service or maintained appropriately.
Workers should understand correct wearing, limitations, inspection and emergency actions.
families.g: Molten-metal PPE risk control depends on metal and splash scenario, quantity and energy, other engineering controls, garment material and fit, contamination, inspection and maintenance, training and supervision.

families.s: HSE surface-engineering process and risk-management guidance
families.t: electroplating, anodising, electropolishing, electroless coating, tinning, metal spraying, enamelling, machinery, chemicals and respiratory health
f: Surface engineering includes electrolytic, electroless, hot-dip, spraying and enamelling processes.
Processes can modify corrosion, wear, appearance and other surface properties.
The sector uses diverse machinery, tanks, chemicals, heat and electrical energy.
Some sites hold significant quantities of toxic substances.
Main health risks include airborne chemicals and sensitising coatings.
Risk assessment should cover each process stage, transfer and maintenance task.
Controls should prioritise substitution, enclosure and ventilation before PPE.
Small subcontract businesses and in-house facilities need the same systematic control of process hazards.
families.g: Surface-engineering risk depends on process and coating, chemicals and inventory, tanks and energy, heat and spray, ventilation, maintenance, waste, competence and emergency arrangements.
